issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind' implies a fragmented, snapshot-like recollection, whereas 'My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed' implies a broadly coherent and detailed memory. That pair is difficult to reconcile as describing the same trauma memory without qualification, making the memory profile internally inconsistent. 'Partial Clarity' could fit with either style, but the simultaneous endorsement of both strongly snapshot-like and globally vivid/detailed memory is the main coherence problem.

vignette: Six months ago, Chloe's boyfriend collapsed in their kitchen, his chest seizing before he hit the linoleum. She performed compressions until the paramedics arrived, and he survived, but the event fractured her sense of safety. Now, her recall of that afternoon arrives as a series of unbidden still frames rather than a continuous narrative. She sees the exact angle of his head against the tile, the slow darkening of his lips, the way the overhead light caught the sweat on his forehead. Yet the interval between his first gasp and the arrival of the sirens is a seamless white void. Her conviction that she misread his distress, that the tragedy occurred because of the way she acted, combined with the growing certainty that people are not what they seem, has directly shaped how the trauma surfaces. The gaps in her recall are no longer neutral blanks; they are interpreted as proof of her inadequacy, while the vivid visual fragments loop with increasing frequency, each image charged with the fear that she failed him. In turn, those relentless visual intrusions continuously pull her back to that kitchen floor. Every time the image of his labored breathing flashes across her mind, it reinforces the conviction that she is responsible and that she cannot rely on other people to keep her safe. Driven by this deep-seated belief that she is at fault and that the world is inherently unreliable, Chloe adopted rigid strategies to manage the perceived threat. She stopped watching television and deleted news apps, avoiding news reports about events similar to what happened to her because they would fracture her composure. She also decided against seeking medical or psychological help, convinced that professionals would merely judge her or fail her. Her avoidance and emotional suppression have only deepened these appraisals. By steering clear of medical coverage and refusing clinical support, she deprives herself of any corrective perspective, leaving her self-blame unchallenged. Her withdrawal from others confirms her fear that she truly cannot rely on anyone, and her need to remain hyper-vigilant grows. The vivid, picture-heavy memories dictate her daily behavior, forcing her to try hard to control her emotions the moment a trigger appears. When the image of his blue-tinged face surfaces, she immediately forces her breathing to steady and masks any tremor in her hands. This compulsion to suppress her distress extends directly into her work as a bartender, where she avoids checking emergency alert notifications or glancing at the overhead televisions in the breakroom. This pattern became untenable during a shift last month when a regular customer suddenly dropped his glass and clutched his chest. Chloe froze as the familiar visual of her boyfriend's collapse superimposed over the patron's face. Instead of acting immediately, she gripped the polishing cloth, forced her features into a neutral mask, and watched until another staff member made the call. After work, she left without her partner, unable to bear the thought of needing to explain her panic. She finally sought help because the gaps in her memory were merging with the gaps in her life, and she hopes to stop controlling every reaction, though she remains terrified that if she stops, the memories will consume her and she will finally have to admit how much she depends on people she no longer believes will stay.
